They stepped forward together onto a path through the grass. Jonah led with his left leg while their hands swung close between them.

“I can’t get that man off my mind.” Mara slowed and looked at him. “You said you could help me talk through sessions. That was true?”

Jonah kept his hand but stepped back to wait until Mara looked ready. “It’s true.”

She heard a quiet calm she hadn’t been ready to ask for.

“When could you be ready to start? Would you meet at your place?”

Mara moved in front of him. Jonah touched her upper arm with his other hand then dropped it. “I can see you starting tomorrow, same time.”

His eyes held her gaze without looking away. Mara wanted to look back and keep holding.

“Is there somewhere we can walk through what I’m feeling right now?” She pulled his hand down from her waist to the small of her back.

Jonah turned so that they faced the pickup with their hands touching. “Do you want to see a beach, or the harbor?” His voice didn’t push. Mara chose by the rhythm in her chest.

They stood on top of a short hill with the ocean just to their right. Jonah was three inches taller and stayed beside her as she looked down at the shore.

He cleared his throat to get her attention but did not move. Mara let him guide the walk.

“Is that it?” Her voice caught in a sharp note. “A little distance from the other session participants?”

Jonah’s eyes said he knew exactly what Mara was feeling. She wanted a moment with someone who didn’t expect her to say a lot.

He took off his glasses, held them at a right angle to his eyes, and handed them toward Mara. She caught them before they could fall and stood waiting.

Jonah nodded and set both hands on top of hers as if they were two palms flat on a desk.

Mara took the glasses and examined the metal frame for signs of sweat or moisture. “Can I keep these?”

“If you want.” His hand moved to her back, right side.

Mara closed her eyes, put on the glasses, and turned away to face the dark.

“Don’t touch me,” Jonah said in a calm, patient voice. “Just stand and breathe while I see if there’s somewhere more comfortable to sit.”

Mara stood still and listened until she felt sure Jonah was farther away. She pushed his hand away, opened her eyes, and walked slowly down the path toward a small stone bench in the grass.

After the session Mara came out to a warm night, dry except for the smell of wet moss under the trees. Jonah was on the front steps beside a black pickup.

Mara turned as he closed the door. “I’ll walk home.”

“Okay.” The low voice didn’t ask for explanations.

Jonah closed his hand on the door’s metal bar and rested beside it. When she stood straight and met his eyes he offered a hand, palm up, wrist steady. His eyes said “I wait for you.”

Mara set her left hand in his and let their fingertips touch without squeezing. He held it with just enough pressure to balance her if she moved. His back straightened and the muscles around his eyes eased as if he’d just taken an easy breath.

They moved together out of the light across the flagstones toward the street. She felt more balanced, more clear in her body.

“Are you cold?” Jonah said when they reached the sidewalk. His hand left hers, but not before she had a chance to register what she felt, as if he waited for her to breathe into her body and experience herself.

“I’ll be okay. Just tired.”

“Want to walk with me, or do you need to be alone?”

“Alone tonight. Thank you.” She tried not to look away first. “You can let go now.”

His fingers released the slight pressure against hers. He kept his hand there, just out of contact, like a pause he was asking for.

He stepped forward, and she moved to follow, but then stopped to watch his back. His shirt was loose and light-colored, not quite faded, almost yellow. His pants were a little looser at the hip than the last time she saw him.

She walked more slowly to avoid catching up. He moved faster than usual, like he wanted the distance between them to grow. Maybe he felt her watching him.

Jonah stopped at an intersection with his back toward her and waited for the light. He was far enough away that she couldn’t see which side of the curb he was standing on. She didn’t know if he would stay there when the light turned green or if he would keep going straight down his street.

She kept walking slowly. As long as she stayed at this intersection she had time to think before she had to cross. She thought about how different it felt in her body now after being touched. She didn’t want to let go of what was left of that contact—the feeling of being warm and protected, held together and alive in one place.

Mara looked up at his back again. He had taken a step off the curb without looking back. He was already turning around when she met his eyes again. His face was tilted slightly away from hers, like he was listening to something behind her that wasn’t there. It made him seem like someone she didn’t know.

His head turned more as if he noticed her watch. He looked toward it and then back to her face. She could see him breathe a little faster through his nose before he breathed slowly in through his mouth, but not deep enough to move his stomach.

Mara turned as he closed the door. “I’ll walk home.”

segment:
The palm of his hand felt warm against Mara’s fingers, dry, smooth-skinned except for calluses where his tools had carved their own imprint. He didn’t let her pull away or rush ahead or hurry him along. When she stopped to wipe sweat from her neck, he kept their hands joined and just waited beside her.

When she was ready, he followed at the same easy pace.

She felt the connection through his hand for nearly a full quarter-mile, a steady weight that carried her forward without effort. She felt him step forward to close gaps and slow down if she stopped to watch birdsong flash in the trees. He held the balance so gently that she noticed only when he eased out.

When he let go she stood still for a moment, palm on the wood rail of the steps leading down to her street. Her arm felt lighter, but it swung in his rhythm. Jonah had left her carrying his beat, his body’s forward momentum. She stepped out and followed it up to the front door.

The lock released with a quiet click. As she opened the door she looked up at him and smiled. The smile turned into a wave as she stepped back inside.

The door clicked closed behind her. When she turned it was closed, the steps empty. He had waited only until she made it safely inside.

Mara leaned against the door and let the cold metal frame cool her shoulders. It felt good to be in her own space. Good to be out of the lab. She hadn’t cried again since she called him “doctor” in the session and heard herself say it. The words had been almost a reflex. They were something she used to protect herself from getting too close, from wanting things she couldn’t have, from risking vulnerability and rejection.

She thought about their walk. Thought about the way she had let him hold her hand without flinching. She wasn’t sure why it felt so good to walk beside him when she usually kept a distance between them. Usually she was too afraid to let herself want things she couldn’t have. But tonight…tonight she felt safe and wanted.

Mara pulled back from the door frame and walked into the living room. The dim light from the kitchen filtered into the dark space where she collapsed on the worn couch. She stared at the ceiling and thought about the session, the experiment, how she’d acted like a patient instead of a fellow researcher, how Jonah had responded with kindness instead of frustration or pity.
